42881: Futurist readers expect a person whose name will fit. Irenaeus (*Against Heresies* 5.30) already warned against confident guessing and offered only cautious suggestions.
42883: Solomon received 666 talents of gold a year just before his fall into idolatry and excess. Some see the beast as power and wealth turned against God. A suggestive parallel, but not proven.
42884: Solomon's yearly gold (1 Kgs 10:14); the 666 sons of Adonikam (Ezra 2:13), which is just a census figure.
42885: Only Rev 13:18. The mark on hand or forehead (Rev 13:16-17) contrasts with God's seal on the foreheads of his servants (Rev 7:3; Rev 14:1) and echoes Deut 6:8, so it is about loyalty and worship, not only a physical mark.
42886: Gematria can make almost any name add to 666 with enough adjustments; popes, emperors, dictators and presidents have all been 'identified'. Treat any precise modern identification as speculative.
42889: A thousand often means 'very many' or 'a vast span'. Its most debated use is the thousand years of Revelation 20, the 'millennium'. Christians read it as a future literal reign, as the present age of the church, or as a coming golden age before Christ returns.
42891: Cattle on a thousand hills; love to a thousand generations. Clearly not counts.
42893: Peter uses this to explain the apparent delay of Christ's return. It is not a formula for 'one day = 1,000 years'.
42894: The millennium as a future literal reign (premillennial)
42895: Christ returns and then reigns for a thousand years on earth before the final judgement. Held by many early Fathers (Papias, Justin, Irenaeus) and by modern premillennialists.
42896: The millennium as the present church age (amillennial)
42897: Satan is bound now (Jesus binds the strong man), and the saints reign with Christ now. Influential through Augustine (*City of God* 20.7-9) and held by many Catholics, Orthodox, Lutherans and Reformed.
42898: A golden age before Christ returns (postmillennial)
42899: The gospel gradually transforms the world, then Christ returns. Strong among Puritans and 19th-century evangelicals; held today by some Reformed writers.
42900: Thousands as large numbers (Exod 20:6; Ps 50:10; Ps 90:4); military units of a thousand (Num 31:4).
42901: 2 Pet 3:8 and Rev 20:2-7, where 'thousand years' appears six times.
42902: Revelation's numbers are often symbolic (seven horns, twelve thousand per tribe), which supports but does not prove a symbolic thousand. Each millennial view has able defenders; see the debate page.
42903: Three and a half (42 months, 1,260 days)
42904: Daniel and Revelation speak of a limited time of trouble in several ways: 'a time, times and half a time', 42 months, and 1,260 days. All equal about three and a half years, half of seven. The idea is a period of real suffering that God has cut short. Readers disagree whether it is a literal future period, a past one, or a symbol for the whole church age.
42905: A broken, limited time of persecution
42906: Half of seven: the enemy's time is real but cut off. This basic meaning is shared across views.
42908: Most critical scholars read Daniel's half-week as the roughly three years when the temple was desecrated (167-164 BC). Many conservative scholars see Daniel looking further ahead as well, or primarily.
42910: Futurists, especially dispensationalists, see the second half of a seven-year tribulation before Christ returns.
42911: The church age between Christ's ascension and return
42912: Idealist and many amillennial readers note the woman flees to the wilderness after the child is taken up to God, so the 1,260 days cover the church's whole wilderness journey.
42914: Historicists (e.g. many Reformers and later Adventists) took each day as a year and dated 1,260 years of papal power. This depends on a debated principle and is little held today outside some traditions.
42915: Daniel's 'time, times and half a time' (Dan 7:25; Dan 12:7) and the half week (Dan 9:27). The 1,290 and 1,335 days (Dan 12:11-12) are unexplained extensions.
42916: Revelation uses all three forms (Rev 11:2-3; Rev 12:6; Rev 12:14; Rev 13:5). Jesus and James say Elijah's drought lasted three years and six months (Luke 4:25; Jas 5:17), while 1 Kgs 18:1 says rain came 'in the third year', perhaps counting from a different point.
42917: Date-setting from these numbers has a long record of failed predictions. Note that Revelation uses three different forms for the same span, which suggests the length is symbolic.
42919: After the resurrection the disciples catch 153 large fish and the net does not tear. John gives the exact number, which has puzzled readers for centuries. It may be an eyewitness memory, a symbol of the whole world's harvest, or a mathematical puzzle; no reading has won general agreement.
42921: Fishermen count and share catches. John stresses eyewitness testimony in the same chapter. Many commentators think this is the simplest explanation, possibly alongside symbolism.
42922: All nations gathered: every kind of fish
42923: Jerome (*Commentary on Ezekiel*, on Ezek 47) says ancient naturalists counted 153 species of fish, so the catch stands for all peoples. The claim about the naturalist (Oppian) does not match surviving texts, so the source is doubtful.
42924: A triangular number: the sum of 1 to 17
42925: Augustine (*Tractates on John* 122.8) notes 153 is 1+2+...+17 and reads 17 as 10 (Law) plus 7 (Spirit). Mathematically true; the meaning he attaches is tradition.
42927: Ezekiel's river from the temple fills the Dead Sea with fish 'from En-gedi to En-eglaim'. J. A. Emerton (1958) proposed that these names produce 17 and 153 by letter-values. Ingenious but speculative.
42928: No OT occurrence; Ezekiel's vision of fishermen (Ezek 47:10) is the most-cited background.
42929: Only John 21:11. Contrast the earlier miraculous catch where the nets begin to break (Luke 5:6).
42930: When a number has had many clever explanations and none prevails, hold all of them lightly. The clear point of the scene is the abundant catch at Jesus' word and the net that holds.
42932: Abraham rescues Lot with 318 trained men. An early Christian writing, the *Epistle of Barnabas*, read 318 in Greek letters as a hidden picture of Jesus and the cross. This is a famous example of ancient gematria, not the plain sense of Genesis.
42934: The plain sense: Abraham's armed servants, born in his household. The number is unusual and specific, which suggests an old record rather than a symbol.
42936: *Barnabas* 9.7-9 notes that in Greek numerals 318 is T (300) plus I and H (18). IH are the first letters of Iesous, and T is shaped like the cross. Note this uses Greek letters, which Abraham did not use, and Barnabas treats circumcision of 318 as the point (combining Gen 14 with Gen 17).
42938: Some rabbinic sources note that the Hebrew letters of Eliezer, Abraham's servant, add to 318, suggesting Abraham went with Eliezer alone. Tradition, and plainly not the narrative's meaning.
42940: Later church tradition gave the number of bishops at the Council of Nicaea (325) as 318 and some writers linked it to Abraham. The actual attendance is uncertain (ancient estimates range from about 250 to 318).
42942: None. The NT does not interpret this number; Hebrews mentions the battle only in passing (Heb 7:1).
42943: Barnabas shows how early Christians sometimes read the Old Testament: by clever wordplay that the original authors could not have meant. Valuable as history of interpretation; not a model for exegesis.
42946: White in the Bible stands for purity, victory and the glory of God. Sins are washed 'white as snow', the transfigured Jesus shines white, and the redeemed in Revelation wear white robes washed in the Lamb's blood.
42948: The paradox of Rev 7:14 (robes made white in blood) shows white is about forgiveness through sacrifice, not natural innocence.
42950: The Ancient of Days has white clothing and hair; Jesus' clothes shine at the transfiguration; the final judgement is from a great white throne.
42951: Victory and righteousness of the saints
42952: Revelation explains the bride's fine linen as 'the righteous deeds of the saints'. White robes are also festal and victory clothing in the Greco-Roman world.
42954: Angels at the tomb and ascension appear in white or shining clothes.
42955: Snow and wool as images of cleansing (Isa 1:18), white garments for joy (Eccl 9:8), white hair of the Ancient of Days (Dan 7:9). In skin-disease laws, white hair or patches could be a sign of uncleanness (Lev 13:3), so white is not always positive.
42956: Transfiguration (Mark 9:3), angels (Matt 28:3), and many uses in Revelation: white robes, white horse, white stone with a new name (Rev 2:17), white cloud (Rev 14:14), white throne (Rev 20:11).
42957: Biblical white imagery is about light and cleanness, not skin colour. Using it to rank human races is a misuse with an ugly history.
42962: Red is the colour of blood, so it carries both life and violence. Scarlet thread or wool appears in cleansing rituals and in Rahab's rescue, while red and scarlet also mark the bloodshed of war and the luxury of Babylon in Revelation.
42964: 'Though your sins be as scarlet.' Scarlet dye was colourfast, so the image is of a stain that will not wash out, except by God.
42966: Scarlet wool with cedar and hyssop was used in purification; the red heifer's ashes cleansed from death. Hebrews gathers these into Christ's work.
42968: Rahab's scarlet cord marks her house for safety. Christian writers from Clement of Rome (*1 Clement* 12) onward saw it as a sign of redemption through blood, recalling the Passover blood on doorposts. Tradition, not the stated meaning.
42970: The red horse takes peace from the earth; the warrior's garments are red as one who treads the winepress.
42972: Babylon rides a scarlet beast and wears purple and scarlet. Soldiers mock Jesus with a scarlet (Matthew) or purple (Mark, John) cloak, parodying royalty.
42973: Scarlet thread on Zerah's hand (Gen 38:28), tabernacle curtains of scarlet yarn (Exod 26:1), purification (Lev 14:4), Esau/Edom the 'red' one (Gen 25:30), a wife clothing her household in scarlet (Prov 31:21).
42974: Scarlet robe at the mocking (Matt 27:28), red horse and red dragon (Rev 6:4; Rev 12:3), scarlet beast and woman (Rev 17:3-4), scarlet wool in Hebrews (Heb 9:19).
42975: A popular sermon links Ps 22:6 ('I am a worm', Hebrew tolaat) to the scarlet-dye insect to picture Christ's blood. The word tolaat is the general word for worm; the connection is speculative.
42980: Purple dye, made from sea snails, was very expensive, so purple meant royalty, wealth and high status. It was woven into the tabernacle and priestly clothes, worn by kings, mocked onto Jesus, and sold by Lydia.
42982: Kings of Midian wore purple; Mordecai and Daniel are honoured with it.
42983: Holiness and beauty of God's dwelling
42984: Blue, purple and scarlet yarn are the standard trio for the tabernacle and priestly garments.
42986: The irony is that the mocked king is the true king.
42987: Wealth that ignores God and neighbour
42988: The rich man in purple ignores Lazarus; Babylon trades in purple.
42989: Tabernacle fabric (Exod 26:1), priestly garments (Exod 28:5), royal dress (Judg 8:26), the capable wife's clothing (Prov 31:22), the lover's hair 'like purple' (Song 7:5).
42990: Jesus' mocking robe (Mark 15:17), the rich man (Luke 16:19), Lydia the seller of purple (Acts 16:14), Babylon (Rev 17:4; Rev 18:16).
42991: Purple itself is neutral; it signals status. Whether that status is honoured or condemned depends on the story.
42995: The Hebrew tekhelet was a costly blue-violet dye. Israelites wore a blue cord on the tassels of their garments to remember God's commands, and the high priest wore a robe all of blue. Jewish tradition linked the colour to sea, sky and God's throne.
42997: The blue thread in the tassels was a visible reminder to obey and not follow one's own heart.
42999: The high priest's robe was all blue; blue cloths covered the holiest furnishings when moved.
43000: Heaven and the throne of God
43001: Under God's feet was a sapphire pavement 'like the very heaven'. The Talmud (*Menachot* 43b) says tekhelet resembles the sea, the sea the sky, and the sky the throne of glory. That chain is tradition.
43002: Tabernacle and priestly fabric (Exod 26:1; Exod 28:31), tassels (Num 15:38), Persian palace hangings (Esth 1:6).
43003: Almost absent as a symbol. Jacinth (hyacinth-blue) appears in breastplates of the demonic cavalry (Rev 9:17) and as a foundation stone (Rev 21:20). Jesus' tassels (Matt 9:20; Matt 14:36) would have had tekhelet if dye was available.
43004: The exact shade and source of tekhelet are debated (most scholars favour a sea snail, Murex trunculus). Ancient colour words do not match modern categories well.
43006: Black in the Bible is mostly linked to mourning, famine, judgement and darkness. It is not used to describe a people as evil; in Song of Songs the woman is 'black and beautiful'.
43008: The black horse carries scales and food prices that mean famine.
43010: Heavens darken and the sun becomes black as sackcloth (dark goat-hair cloth worn in mourning).
43012: 'Blackness of darkness' (KJV) describes the fate of false teachers.
43013: Simple description of beauty or health
43014: The woman is sun-darkened and beautiful; the beloved's hair is black as a raven; black hair can show healing.
43015: Darkened skin from suffering (Job 30:30; Lam 4:8), darkened heavens (Jer 4:28), horses in Zechariah's vision (Zech 6:2; Zech 6:6), sunburnt beauty (Song 1:5).
43016: Hair black or white (Matt 5:36), the black horse (Rev 6:5), the black sun (Rev 6:12), blackness of darkness (Jude 1:13).
43017: The so-called 'curse of Ham' used to justify racial slavery misreads Gen 9:25: the curse falls on Canaan, and nothing is said about skin colour. Biblical darkness imagery is about light and its absence, not ethnicity.
43021: Green is the colour of life, growth and God's provision: green pastures, green leaves of the righteous. Because pagan shrines were often under leafy trees, 'under every green tree' became a phrase for idolatry.
43023: God gives green plants for food; the shepherd leads to green pastures. Mark notes the green grass at the feeding, perhaps an eyewitness touch of springtime.
43025: Trees that stay green in drought picture those who trust God.
43027: Hill-top shrines and sacred trees; 'under every green tree' became a formula.
43029: 'If they do this when the wood is green, what will happen when it is dry?' Most read it as: if the innocent Jesus suffers so, how much worse for guilty Jerusalem. Exact sense debated.
43030: Green plants for food (Gen 1:30), green pastures (Ps 23:2), the wicked flourishing like a green tree only for a time (Ps 37:35), idolatrous groves (Deut 12:2).
43031: Green grass (Mark 6:39; Rev 8:7; Rev 9:4), green and dry wood (Luke 23:31). The same Greek word chlōros is the 'pale' horse of Rev 6:8.
43032: Green is not a liturgical or mystical code in Scripture; church calendars using green for 'ordinary time' are later tradition.
43037: Gold stands for the highest value, royal splendour and the glory of God's presence. The holiest objects in the tabernacle and temple were gold, and the new Jerusalem is pure gold like clear glass. Gold can also become an idol, as with the golden calf.
43039: The ark, lampstand and inner temple were gold. The whole new city is gold, as though the holy of holies now fills everything (it is also cube-shaped, Rev 21:16, like the holy of holies in 1 Kgs 6:20).
43041: The head of gold is Babylon; the magi bring gold to a king; elders wear golden crowns. Irenaeus (*Against Heresies* 3.9.2) and later Fathers read the gold as a sign of kingship, incense of deity and myrrh of death; tradition.
43043: Gold is purified by fire; faith tested by trials is more precious.
43045: The golden calf and Nebuchadnezzar's golden statue; hoarded gold that corrodes.
43046: Tabernacle furnishings (Exod 25), Solomon's temple (1 Kgs 6:22), wisdom better than gold (Prov 8:19), God's words sweeter and more desirable than gold (Ps 19:10), 'the gold is mine' (Hag 2:8).
43047: Magi's gift (Matt 2:11), tested faith (1 Pet 1:7), golden lampstands and sash (Rev 1:12-13), golden bowls of incense as prayers (Rev 5:8), the golden city (Rev 21:18).
43048: Gold as a metal and precious stone is covered separately under metals and stones. Prosperity readings that treat gold streets as a promise of present wealth misread the vision.
43050: The fourth horse in Revelation is chlōros, the same word used for green grass. Here it means the sickly grey-green of a corpse. Its rider is named Death, and Hades follows. The colour itself signals death and disease.
43052: Death kills by sword, famine, pestilence and wild beasts, echoing Ezekiel's four judgements.
43054: Authority is 'given' over a quarter of the earth: the judgement is real but bounded by God.
43055: Terror and sickness on the face
43056: Hebrew speaks of faces turning pale or greenish (yeraqon) in terror.
43057: Faces turning pale with fear (Jer 30:6); horses of different colours patrolling the earth in Zechariah (Zech 1:8; Zech 6:2-3), the background for Revelation's four horses.
43058: Only Rev 6:8 as a horse colour; chlōros elsewhere means green (Mark 6:39; Rev 8:7; Rev 9:4).
43059: Linking the pale horse to a particular modern pandemic or to Islam (because of green flags) is speculative. Revelation's horsemen describe recurring realities of war, famine and death.
43062: Lambs were the common sacrifice in Israel, above all at Passover. John the Baptist calls Jesus 'the Lamb of God who takes away the sin of the world', and Revelation's central figure is a Lamb standing as though slain, who is also the conquering ruler.
43063: The Passover lamb and rescue from death
43064: The lamb's blood marked the houses spared. John notes Jesus' bones were not broken, like the Passover lamb; Paul calls Christ 'our Passover'.
43065: The suffering servant led to slaughter
43066: Philip applies Isa 53 to Jesus. 'A lamb without blemish' combines the sacrificial requirement with sinlessness.
43068: Abraham's words on Moriah are widely read by Christians as pointing to Christ. Jewish tradition reflects deeply on Isaac's binding (the Aqedah). The link to John 1:29 is a common typology, not stated in John.
43069: Which lamb is the 'Lamb of God'?
43070: Scholars debate whether John means the Passover lamb, the servant of Isa 53, the daily temple lamb (tamid), the lamb of Gen 22, or a warrior-lamb of Jewish apocalyptic (as in *1 Enoch* 89-90). Many think several are combined.
43072: John hears of a Lion and sees a Lamb (Rev 5:5-6): Christ conquers by self-giving death. The Lamb is worshipped, shepherds, judges, marries his bride and lights the city.
43073: Abel's offering of the flock (Gen 4:4), Passover (Exod 12), daily morning and evening lambs (Num 28:3-4), the servant as a lamb (Isa 53:7), the wolf lying with the lamb (Isa 11:6; Isa 65:25).
43074: John the Baptist's witness (John 1:29), Philip and the eunuch (Acts 8:32), Christ our Passover (1 Cor 5:7), the blameless lamb (1 Pet 1:19), and nearly thirty times in Revelation (arnion). Disciples as lambs among wolves (Luke 10:3) and Jesus' 'feed my lambs' (John 21:15).
43075: Revelation's beast from the earth has 'two horns like a lamb' (Rev 13:11): a lamb-like look is no guarantee of truth. Passover was not formally a sin offering, so the NT's lamb imagery blends several sacrifices rather than mapping one-to-one.
43079: Lions lived in ancient Israel and were the most feared predator. The lion stands for royal strength (the Lion of Judah), for God's roaring judgement, and also for deadly enemies, including the devil 'like a roaring lion'. The same animal can picture God or his enemies.
43080: Royal power of Judah and the Messiah
43081: Jacob's blessing calls Judah a lion's cub with the sceptre. Revelation names Jesus 'the Lion of the tribe of Judah'.
43083: 'The lion has roared; who will not fear?' God is like a lion against his unfaithful people, and also roars to gather them home.
43085: Persecutors and Satan are lions that devour. Paul was 'rescued from the lion's mouth', probably meaning a lethal danger rather than literal lions.
43087: 'The righteous are bold as a lion.'
43088: A face of the throne creatures and a Gospel symbol
43089: One of the four faces. Later tradition linked the lion to Mark (Jerome) or to John (Irenaeus); tradition varies.
43090: Samson and David kill lions (Judg 14:5-6; 1 Sam 17:34-37), a disobedient prophet killed by a lion (1 Kgs 13:24), Daniel in the den (Dan 6:22), Babylon as a winged lion (Dan 7:4), the lion eating straw in the peaceable kingdom (Isa 11:7).
43091: The devil as a roaring lion (1 Pet 5:8), the faithful who shut lions' mouths (Heb 11:33), the Lion of Judah (Rev 5:5), a lion-like beast (Rev 13:2).
43092: C. S. Lewis's Aslan has made the lion a popular Christ image; that is a modern literary use. In Scripture the lion is morally neutral, and context decides.
43093: Doves were gentle, common birds and the poor family's sacrifice. A dove brought Noah the olive leaf, and the Spirit descended on Jesus 'like a dove' at his baptism. Doves also picture innocence, love, mourning and, in Hosea, silliness.
43095: All four Gospels use the image; Luke says 'in bodily form like a dove'. Some link it to the Spirit hovering over the waters (Gen 1:2), which rabbinic tradition likened to a hovering dove (Talmud *Hagigah* 15a). That connection is tradition.
43096: New creation and peace after judgement
43097: The dove finds no rest, then returns with an olive leaf. The modern peace symbol of dove and olive branch grew from this story.
43099: Mary and Joseph offer the poor family's sacrifice. Temple dove-sellers were driven out by Jesus (Matt 21:12).
43101: 'Wise as serpents, innocent as doves.' The beloved is 'my dove'.
43103: Ephraim is a silly dove flitting between Egypt and Assyria; doves' cooing sounds like moaning.
43104: Noah's dove (Gen 8:8-12), Abraham's covenant offering (Gen 15:9), poor offerings (Lev 12:8), longing for dove's wings (Ps 55:6), Jonah's name means dove (Jonah 1:1), exiles returning like doves (Hos 11:11).
43105: Jesus' baptism (Matt 3:16), sacrifice for Jesus' presentation (Luke 2:24), temple sellers (John 2:14), innocence (Matt 10:16).
43106: Some preachers make Jonah ('dove') a type of the Spirit or of Israel; that is a name-based link with little textual support.
43109: The serpent in Eden deceives Eve and is cursed, and Revelation names 'that ancient serpent, called the devil and Satan'. Yet the same image is used for healing: the bronze serpent Moses lifted up, which Jesus compares to his own lifting up on the cross.
43110: Deceiver and enemy of God's people
43111: Genesis does not name the serpent as Satan; later Jewish writing (*Wisdom of Solomon* 2:24) and the NT make that identification. Gen 3:15 has been read since Irenaeus as the first gospel promise (the 'protoevangelium'); many modern scholars read it more generally as lasting conflict between humans and evil.
43112: Healing through what was lifted up
43113: Looking at the bronze serpent healed the bitten. Jesus uses it of his crucifixion.
43114: An object that became an idol
43115: Hezekiah smashed the bronze serpent (called Nehushtan) because people burned incense to it. Good symbols can become idols.
43117: The serpent was 'crafty' (Hebrew arum, a pun on 'naked', arummim, in Gen 2:25). Jesus tells disciples to be wise as serpents, without guile.
43119: Disciples tread on serpents; Paul shakes off a viper. Mark 16:18 also mentions handling snakes, but that is in the longer ending of Mark, missing from the earliest manuscripts.
